# Arabic Alphabet & Letter Forms

Arabic has 28 letters, all consonants. The script is written right-to-left, and most letters change shape depending on their position in the word: isolated, initial, medial, or final.

## Core Vocabulary (the alphabet)

| Letter | romanization | name | sound |
|--------|--------------|------|-------|
| ا | ā / a | alif | long "a" / glottal carrier |
| ب | b | bāʾ | "b" |
| ت | t | tāʾ | "t" |
| ث | th | thāʾ | "th" as in think |
| ج | j | jīm | "j" (or "g" in Egyptian) |
| ح | ḥ | ḥāʾ | breathy "h" (deep) |
| خ | kh | khāʾ | like German "Bach" |
| د | d | dāl | "d" |
| ذ | dh | dhāl | "th" as in this |
| ر | r | rāʾ | rolled "r" |
| ز | z | zāy | "z" |
| س | s | sīn | "s" |
| ش | sh | shīn | "sh" |
| ص | ṣ | ṣād | emphatic "s" |
| ض | ḍ | ḍād | emphatic "d" |
| ط | ṭ | ṭāʾ | emphatic "t" |
| ظ | ẓ | ẓāʾ | emphatic "th/z" |
| ع | ʿ | ʿayn | voiced pharyngeal — no English match |
| غ | gh | ghayn | French "r" / gargled "g" |
| ف | f | fāʾ | "f" |
| ق | q | qāf | uvular "k" (back of throat) |
| ك | k | kāf | "k" |
| ل | l | lām | "l" |
| م | m | mīm | "m" |
| ن | n | nūn | "n" |
| ه | h | hāʾ | light "h" as in hat |
| و | w / ū | wāw | "w" / long "oo" |
| ي | y / ī | yāʾ | "y" / long "ee" |

## Example Words

- **بَيْت** (bayt) — house
- **كِتاب** (kitāb) — book
- **وَلَد** (walad) — boy
- **بِنْت** (bint) — girl
- **شَمْس** (shams) — sun
- **قَمَر** (qamar) — moon

## Script Notes

- **Right-to-left**: read and write from right.
- **Connecting letters**: 22 of 28 letters connect to the next letter. Six "non-connectors" (ا د ذ ر ز و) connect from the right but never to the left.
- **Four shapes per letter**: isolated, initial (start of word), medial (middle), final. Example for ب: ب / بـ / ـبـ / ـب.
- **No capitals**: Arabic has no uppercase/lowercase distinction.
- **Numerals**: Modern Arabic numerals (٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩) are written left-to-right within a right-to-left text.

## Common Mistakes

- Confusing ح / خ / ج — same skeleton, different dots. Count and place dots carefully.
- Treating ع as a vowel — it's a consonant (voiced pharyngeal).
- Missing the difference between س (sīn, three teeth) and ش (shīn, three teeth + three dots).

## Try It Yourself

1. Write the alphabet in isolated form once.
2. Identify the four shapes of ب and ت in a word.
3. Spot the six non-connectors in بِنْت (bint) and بَلَد (balad).
4. Practice writing your name in Arabic letters.

## Next Steps

You can recognize the letters. Next: vowels — short ones are diacritics, long ones are letters.

# Short & Long Vowels

Arabic has three vowel sounds — a, i, u — each in a short form (a small mark above or below a letter) and a long form (a full letter: ا و ي). Short vowels are often omitted in everyday writing.

## Short Vowels (Ḥarakāt)

| Mark | name | sound | example |
|------|------|-------|---------|
| ـَ | fatḥa | short "a" | كَتَبَ (kataba — he wrote) |
| ـِ | kasra | short "i" | كِتاب (kitāb — book) |
| ـُ | ḍamma | short "u" | كُتُب (kutub — books) |
| ـْ | sukūn | no vowel | بَيْت (bayt — house) |
| ـّ | shadda | doubled consonant | دَرَّسَ (darrasa — he taught) |
| ـً ـٍ ـٌ | tanwīn | -an / -in / -un (indefinite case ending) | كِتابٌ (kitābun — a book) |

## Long Vowels

| Letter | sound | example |
|--------|-------|---------|
| ا | long "ā" | كِتاب (kitāb) |
| و | long "ū" | نُور (nūr — light) |
| ي | long "ī" | فِيل (fīl — elephant) |

## Example Sentences

- **هذا كِتابٌ.** (hādhā kitābun.) — This is a book.
- **هذه بِنْتٌ.** (hādhihi bintun.) — This is a girl.
- **بَيْتي كَبيرٌ.** (baytī kabīrun.) — My house is big.
- **هو كَتَبَ كِتاباً.** (huwa kataba kitāban.) — He wrote a book.

## Grammar Notes

- **Vowel marks (taшkīl)** are used in the Qurʾān, children's books, language textbooks, and dictionaries. Newspapers and adult prose drop them — readers are expected to supply them.
- **Long vs short** changes meaning: كَتَبَ (kataba — wrote) vs كاتِب (kātib — writer).
- **Shadda doubles a consonant** and is grammatically meaningful: دَرَسَ (he studied) vs دَرَّسَ (he taught).
- **Tanwīn** appears only on indefinite nouns: كِتابٌ (a book) vs الكِتابُ (the book).

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing every long ā as short — this changes word meaning.
- Skipping shadda — single vs doubled consonant differs in meaning.
- Mistaking ـة (tāʾ marbūṭa) for a vowel — it's a special "t" that marks feminine endings.

## Try It Yourself

1. Add fatḥa, kasra, or ḍamma to read: كتب, بنت, ولد.
2. Distinguish kataba (he wrote) from kutiba (it was written) — only vowel marks differ.
3. Identify long vowels in: قَمَر, نُور, شَمس, كِتاب.
4. Write your name with full taшkīl.

## Next Steps

Vowels in place. Next: the trickiest part of Arabic pronunciation — emphatic and pharyngeal sounds.
ar-bp-3:
# Pronunciation: Emphatic & Unique Sounds

Arabic has consonants no European language uses: emphatics (ص ض ط ظ), pharyngeals (ح ع), uvulars (ق غ خ), and the glottal stop (ء). Mastering them is the key to sounding natural.

## Core Sounds

| Letter | romanization | description | contrast |
|--------|--------------|-------------|----------|
| ص | ṣ | emphatic s, tongue lowered | vs س (plain s) |
| ض | ḍ | emphatic d | vs د (plain d) |
| ط | ṭ | emphatic t | vs ت (plain t) |
| ظ | ẓ | emphatic dh/z | vs ذ |
| ح | ḥ | voiceless pharyngeal — squeeze throat | vs ه (light h) |
| ع | ʿ | voiced pharyngeal — like ḥ but voiced | unique |
| خ | kh | voiceless uvular fricative | German "Bach" |
| غ | gh | voiced uvular fricative | French "r" |
| ق | q | voiceless uvular stop, deep "k" | vs ك (front k) |
| ء | ʾ | glottal stop | "uh-oh" |

## Minimal Pairs

| Plain | Emphatic | Meaning |
|-------|----------|---------|
| سَيْف (sayf) | صَيْف (ṣayf) | sword / summer |
| تين (tīn) | طين (ṭīn) | figs / mud |
| دَلَّ (dalla) | ضَلَّ (ḍalla) | indicated / went astray |
| هَوى (hawā) | حَوى (ḥawā) | passion / contained |

## Example Words

- **عَرَبي** (ʿarabī) — Arabic / Arab
- **حَبيب** (ḥabīb) — beloved
- **خُبْز** (khubz) — bread
- **غُرْفة** (ghurfa) — room
- **قَلْب** (qalb) — heart
- **مُسْلِم** (muslim) — Muslim

## Pronunciation Tips

- **Emphatics**: pull your tongue root back; the surrounding vowels darken (a → "aw," i → "uh").
- **ع (ʿayn)**: imagine being slightly choked — squeeze the throat without making a "g."
- **ح (ḥāʾ)**: like exhaling on a cold mirror, but harder.
- **ق vs ك**: ق is way back in the throat; ك is at the soft palate.
- **ء (hamza)**: a hard glottal stop — pause-then-release like in "uh-oh."

## Common Mistakes

- Saying ḥ as English "h" — too light.
- Skipping ʿayn or replacing it with "a" — this loses meaning. ʿarabī ≠ "arabī."
- Pronouncing ق as "k" — sounds dialectal or sloppy in MSA.
- Failing to round vowels around emphatics: ṣayf is closer to "sof" than "sef."

## Try It Yourself

1. Practice ʿayn in عَين (ʿayn — "eye"). Squeeze the throat.
2. Contrast ت vs ط in تين / طين.
3. Read aloud: حَبيب, خُبْز, غُرْفة, قَلْب, عَرَبي.
4. Record yourself and compare to a native (Forvo.com).

## Next Steps

Now apply these sounds to grammar — gender, definiteness, plurals.

# Noun Gender, Definiteness & Plurals

Every Arabic noun is either masculine or feminine. Definiteness is marked by the prefix الـ (al-), and Arabic has three numbers — singular, dual, and plural — with two plural types: sound and broken.

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English | gender |
|--------|--------------|---------|--------|
| كِتاب | kitāb | book | m. |
| قَلَم | qalam | pen | m. |
| بَيْت | bayt | house | m. |
| وَلَد | walad | boy | m. |
| مَدْرَسة | madrasa | school | f. |
| سَيّارة | sayyāra | car | f. |
| مَدينة | madīna | city | f. |
| بِنْت | bint | girl | f. |
| الكِتاب | al-kitāb | the book | def. |
| كِتابٌ | kitābun | a book | indef. |
| كِتابانِ | kitābāni | two books | dual |
| كُتُب | kutub | books (broken pl.) | pl. |
| مُدَرِّسون | mudarrisūn | teachers (m. sound pl.) | pl. |
| مُدَرِّسات | mudarrisāt | teachers (f. sound pl.) | pl. |

## Example Sentences

- **هذا كِتابٌ.** (hādhā kitābun.) — This is a book.
- **هذا الكِتابُ جَديدٌ.** (hādhā al-kitābu jadīdun.) — This book is new.
- **عِنْدي قَلَمانِ.** (ʿindī qalamāni.) — I have two pens.
- **في المَدينةِ مَدارِسُ كَثيرة.** (fī al-madīnati madārisu kathīra.) — In the city are many schools.
- **المُدَرِّسونَ في الصَفِّ.** (al-mudarrisūna fī aṣ-ṣaffi.) — The teachers are in the classroom.

## Grammar Notes

- **Feminine marker**: most feminine nouns end in ـة (tāʾ marbūṭa). مَدْرَسة, سَيّارة. Pronounce as "-a" in pause, "-at" before another word.
- **Definite article الـ**: prefixed directly. الـ + شَمس → الشَّمس. The "l" assimilates into "sun letters" (د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن ت ث).
- **Sun vs moon letters**: with sun letters, double the consonant (ash-shams). With moon letters, l stays clear (al-qamar).
- **Dual**: add ـانِ (nominative) or ـَيْنِ (acc./gen.). كِتابانِ, كِتابَيْنِ.
- **Sound masculine plural**: ـونَ / ـينَ (case-dependent).
- **Sound feminine plural**: ـات.
- **Broken plurals** are irregular and must be memorized: كِتاب → كُتُب; قَلَم → أقلام.

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing ـة as "h" — it's "-a" in pause, "-at" linked.
- Forgetting sun-letter assimilation: writing "al-shams" but pronouncing "ash-shams."
- Defaulting all plurals to sound — most nouns take broken plurals.

## Try It Yourself

1. Add الـ to: شَمس, قَمَر, كِتاب, مَدينة. Mark sun vs moon.
2. Make duals: قَلَم → ?, مَدْرَسة → ?
3. Memorize 5 broken plurals.
4. Identify gender: شَمس, قَمَر, طاوِلة, بَيْت.

## Next Steps

Nouns ready. Next: how Arabic builds basic sentences — equational and verbal.

# Basic Sentence Types

Arabic has two basic sentence types: nominal (jumla ismiyya) — starts with a noun, often expresses being or description; and verbal (jumla fiʿliyya) — starts with a verb. The verb-subject order is typical in MSA.

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| هو | huwa | he |
| هي | hiya | she |
| أنا | anā | I |
| أنتَ / أنتِ | anta / anti | you (m / f) |
| نحن | naḥnu | we |
| هذا / هذه | hādhā / hādhihi | this (m / f) |
| ذلك / تلك | dhālika / tilka | that (m / f) |
| هنا | hunā | here |
| هناك | hunāka | there |
| كَبير / كَبيرة | kabīr / kabīra | big (m / f) |
| صَغير / صَغيرة | ṣaghīr / ṣaghīra | small |
| في | fī | in |
| على | ʿalā | on |
| مع | maʿa | with |
| مُدَرِّس | mudarris | teacher |
| طالِب | ṭālib | student |
| جامِعة | jāmiʿa | university |

## Example Sentences (Nominal)

- **هذا بَيْتٌ.** (hādhā baytun.) — This is a house.
- **هي طالِبةٌ.** (hiya ṭālibatun.) — She is a student.
- **البَيْتُ كَبيرٌ.** (al-baytu kabīrun.) — The house is big.
- **الكِتابُ على الطاوِلةِ.** (al-kitābu ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwilati.) — The book is on the table.
- **أنا في البَيْتِ.** (anā fī al-bayti.) — I am at home.

## Example Sentences (Verbal)

- **يَكْتُبُ الوَلَدُ.** (yaktubu al-waladu.) — The boy writes. (V-S)
- **ذَهَبَ المُدَرِّسُ إلى الجامِعةِ.** (dhahaba al-mudarrisu ilā al-jāmiʿati.) — The teacher went to the university.
- **تَقْرَأُ البِنْتُ كِتاباً.** (taqraʾu al-bintu kitāban.) — The girl reads a book.

## Grammar Notes

- **No "to be" in present tense**: "He is a student" → هو طالِبٌ (literally "he student").
- **Nominal sentences** name a topic and a comment, both in nominative case.
- **Verbal sentences** start with the verb. The verb agrees with the subject in gender but stays singular when the subject follows: ذَهَبَ المُدَرِّسونَ — "the (male) teachers went."
- **Adjectives follow the noun** and agree in gender, number, definiteness, and case: البَيْتُ الكَبيرُ — "the big house."
- **Definite + indefinite predicate** = full sentence: البَيْتُ كَبيرٌ — "The house is big" (definite subject + indefinite predicate).

## Common Mistakes

- Inserting "is/am/are" — Arabic doesn't use them in present tense.
- Forgetting adjective agreement: البَيْتُ الكَبيرة — should be الكَبيرُ.
- Confusing definite-definite (= noun phrase) vs definite-indefinite (= sentence).

## Try It Yourself

1. Translate: "I am a student." "She is in the school." "The book is new."
2. Build a nominal sentence with هذا.
3. Write a verbal sentence: "The boy wrote a letter."
4. Add an adjective: "the small car," "a big book."

## Next Steps

Nominal sentences master "to be" without a verb. Next: present-tense conjugation.

# Present Tense Conjugation

Arabic verbs conjugate through prefixes and suffixes around a three-letter root. The present tense (al-muḍāriʿ) uses prefixes: أ (I), ت (you/she), ي (he), ن (we).

## Core Vocabulary

| Root | Verb (3 m.s. past / present) | Meaning |
|------|------------------------------|---------|
| ك ت ب | كَتَبَ / يَكْتُبُ | to write |
| د ر س | دَرَسَ / يَدْرُسُ | to study |
| ذ ه ب | ذَهَبَ / يَذْهَبُ | to go |
| ق ر أ | قَرَأَ / يَقْرَأُ | to read |
| س ك ن | سَكَنَ / يَسْكُنُ | to live (reside) |
| ع م ل | عَمِلَ / يَعْمَلُ | to work |
| ف ع ل | فَعَلَ / يَفْعَلُ | to do |
| س م ع | سَمِعَ / يَسْمَعُ | to hear |
| ش ر ب | شَرِبَ / يَشْرَبُ | to drink |
| أ ك ل | أَكَلَ / يَأْكُلُ | to eat |

## Conjugation Pattern (يَكْتُبُ — to write)

| Pronoun | Form | romanization |
|---------|------|--------------|
| أنا | أَكْتُبُ | aktubu (I write) |
| أنتَ | تَكْتُبُ | taktubu (you m. write) |
| أنتِ | تَكْتُبينَ | taktubīna (you f. write) |
| هو | يَكْتُبُ | yaktubu (he writes) |
| هي | تَكْتُبُ | taktubu (she writes) |
| نحن | نَكْتُبُ | naktubu (we write) |
| أنتم | تَكْتُبونَ | taktubūna (you m.pl.) |
| أنتن | تَكْتُبْنَ | taktubna (you f.pl.) |
| هم | يَكْتُبونَ | yaktubūna (they m.) |
| هن | يَكْتُبْنَ | yaktubna (they f.) |

## Example Sentences

- **أنا أَدْرُسُ العَرَبيّةَ.** (anā adrusu al-ʿarabiyyata.) — I study Arabic.
- **هي تَقْرَأُ كِتاباً.** (hiya taqraʾu kitāban.) — She reads a book.
- **نَحْنُ نَسْكُنُ في القاهِرة.** (naḥnu naskunu fī al-Qāhira.) — We live in Cairo.
- **هم يَذْهَبونَ إلى المَدْرَسة.** (hum yadhhabūna ilā al-madrasa.) — They go to school.
- **ماذا تَفْعَلُ؟** (mādhā tafʿalu?) — What are you doing?

## Grammar Notes

- The present tense covers both "I write" and "I am writing" — context tells you which.
- The middle vowel of the present can be a, i, or u and must be memorized per verb: يَكْتُبُ (u), يَدْرُسُ (u), يَعْمَلُ (a), يَجْلِسُ (i).
- Subject pronouns are usually omitted because the verb form already shows the subject.
- The final ـُ (ḍamma) marks the indicative mood; it changes for subjunctive (ـَ) and jussive (sukūn).

## Common Mistakes

- Mixing prefixes: writing يـ for "you" — should be تـ.
- Forgetting feminine plural ـْنَ — different from masculine plural ـونَ.
- Memorizing the past tense alone — present must be learned with it because the middle vowel is unpredictable.

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate يَدْرُسُ in all 10 forms.
2. Translate: "He drinks tea," "We work in a hospital," "Do they study Arabic?"
3. Drop the pronoun and rely on the verb: instead of "أنا أكتب," just say "أكتب."
4. Make 3 questions using ماذا (what) + verb.

## Next Steps

Verbs in motion. Now build vocabulary through Arabic's most powerful feature — the root system.

# Root System & Word Families

Most Arabic words come from a three-letter root. By inserting vowels and adding prefixes/suffixes through fixed templates, the root produces dozens of related words. Mastering this system multiplies your vocabulary fast.

## Core Concept: the Root كَتَبَ (k-t-b)

| Form | Arabic | romanization | meaning |
|------|--------|--------------|---------|
| Verb (he wrote) | كَتَبَ | kataba | wrote |
| Verb (he is writing) | يَكْتُبُ | yaktubu | writes |
| Verbal noun | كِتابة | kitāba | (the act of) writing |
| Active participle | كاتِب | kātib | writer / one writing |
| Passive participle | مَكْتوب | maktūb | written / a letter |
| Place noun | مَكْتَب | maktab | office / desk |
| Place noun | مَكْتَبة | maktaba | library / bookstore |
| Object | كِتاب | kitāb | book |
| Plural | كُتُب | kutub | books |

All from k-t-b. The pattern tells you the function; the root tells you the meaning.

## Other Productive Roots

### د ر س (d-r-s) — to study

| Word | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| دَرَسَ (darasa) | he studied |
| دَرَّسَ (darrasa) | he taught (Form II) |
| دَرْس (dars) | lesson |
| مَدْرَسة (madrasa) | school |
| مُدَرِّس (mudarris) | teacher |
| دِراسة (dirāsa) | study (n.) |

### ع ل م (ʿ-l-m) — to know

| Word | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| عَلِمَ (ʿalima) | he knew |
| عَلَّمَ (ʿallama) | he taught |
| عِلْم (ʿilm) | knowledge / science |
| عالِم (ʿālim) | scholar |
| مُعَلِّم (muʿallim) | teacher |
| مَعْلوم (maʿlūm) | known |

### ك ل م (k-l-m) — to speak

| Word | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| تَكَلَّمَ (takallama) | he spoke |
| كَلِمة (kalima) | word |
| كَلام (kalām) | speech |
| مُتَكَلِّم (mutakallim) | speaker |

## Common Templates

| Template | Meaning | Example |
|----------|---------|---------|
| فَعَلَ | basic verb (past) | كَتَبَ (wrote) |
| فاعِل | active participle / doer | كاتِب (writer) |
| مَفْعول | passive participle | مَكْتوب (written) |
| مَفْعَل / مَفْعِل | place / time | مَكْتَب (office), مَجْلِس (council) |
| فَعّال | intensive doer | كَذّاب (liar), خَبّاز (baker) |
| فِعالة | abstract noun | كِتابة (writing), دِراسة (studying) |

## Common Mistakes

- Memorizing words in isolation — instead, learn them by root cluster.
- Confusing similar roots: ك ت ب vs ك ت م (to conceal).
- Overgeneralizing patterns — not every root takes every template.

## Try It Yourself

1. From س ك ن (to dwell), guess: سَكَنَ, ساكِن, مَسْكَن, سَكينة.
2. Group these by root: كاتِب, مَكْتَب, كِتاب, كاتِبة.
3. Predict the meaning of مُعَلِّم if عَلَّمَ = he taught.
4. Pick a new word and find three root-mates.

## Next Steps

Root mastery is exponential. Now build active daily vocabulary.

# Greetings, Family & Daily Life

Arabic greetings are warm and elaborate. A simple "hi" can spawn a dozen exchanges. Family vocabulary is the most-used set in any conversation.

## Core Vocabulary — Greetings

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| السَّلامُ عَلَيْكُم | as-salāmu ʿalaykum | peace be upon you (greeting) |
| وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلام | wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām | and upon you peace (reply) |
| مَرْحَباً | marḥaban | hello |

## Core Vocabulary — Family & Daily Life

## Example Sentences

- **السَّلامُ عَلَيْكُم! كَيْفَ حالُك؟** (as-salāmu ʿalaykum! kayfa ḥāluk?) — Peace be upon you! How are you?
- **أنا بِخَيْر، الحَمْدُ لِلّه.** (anā bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh.) — I am well, thanks to God.
- **عائِلَتي صَغيرة: أبي وأمّي وأخي.** (ʿāʾilatī ṣaghīra: abī wa-ummī wa-akhī.) — My family is small: my father, mother, and brother.
- **هذا صَديقي أحمد.** (hādhā ṣadīqī Aḥmad.) — This is my friend Ahmad.
- **أُريد قَهْوة، من فَضْلِك.** (urīdu qahwa, min faḍlik.) — I'd like a coffee, please.

## Grammar Notes

- **Possession via suffix**: my (-ī), your m. (-uka), your f. (-uki), his (-uhu), her (-uhā). أبي = "my father."
- **Religious phrases pepper speech**: الحَمْدُ لِلّه (thanks be to God), إن شاء الله (God willing), ما شاء الله (what God wills) — used by Muslims and many non-Muslim Arabs alike.
- **Greetings are gendered**: kayfa ḥāluk (m) / kayfa ḥāluki (f).

## Common Mistakes

- Replying to السلام عليكم with anything except وعليكم السلام.
- Forgetting to gender the greeting.
- Thinking أب = "father" in citation form: actually أب is rare alone; you'll see أبي ("my father") more often.

## Try It Yourself

1. Greet someone formally and reply.
2. Introduce three family members using possessive suffixes.
3. Ask "How are you?" to a man and a woman.
4. Order a coffee politely.

## Next Steps

# Numbers, Time & Calendar

Arabic numbers behave bizarrely: numerals 3-10 take the opposite gender of the noun (polarity), and the noun's case changes with the count. Two calendars are in use: Hijri (lunar Islamic) and Gregorian.

## Core Vocabulary — Numbers

| ٢ | اِثْنان / اِثْنَتان | ithnān / ithnatān | two |
| ٣ | ثَلاثة / ثَلاث | thalātha / thalāth | three |
| ٤ | أَرْبَعة / أَرْبَع | arbaʿa / arbaʿ | four |
| ٥ | خَمْسة / خَمْس | khamsa / khams | five |
| ٦ | سِتّة / سِتّ | sitta / sitt | six |
| ٧ | سَبْعة / سَبْع | sabʿa / sabʿ | seven |
| ٨ | ثَمانية / ثَمان | thamāniya / thamān | eight |
| ٩ | تِسْعة / تِسْع | tisʿa / tisʿ | nine |
| ١٠ | عَشَرة / عَشْر | ʿashara / ʿashr | ten |
| ١٠٠ | مِئة | miʾa | hundred |
| ١٠٠٠ | أَلْف | alf | thousand |

## Core Vocabulary — Time & Calendar

| Arabic | romanization | English |

| دَقيقة | daqīqa | minute |
| الآن | al-ān | now |
| اليَوْم | al-yawm | today |
| غَداً | ghadan | tomorrow |
| أَمْس | ams | yesterday |
| أُسْبوع | usbūʿ | week |
| شَهْر | shahr | month |
| سَنة | sana | year |
| الأَحَد | al-aḥad | Sunday |
| الاِثْنَيْن | al-ithnayn | Monday |
| الثُّلاثاء | ath-thulāthāʾ | Tuesday |
| الأَرْبِعاء | al-arbiʿāʾ | Wednesday |
| الخَميس | al-khamīs | Thursday |
| الجُمُعة | al-jumuʿa | Friday |
| السَّبْت | as-sabt | Saturday |
| يَناير | yanāyir | January |
| فِبْراير | fibrāyir | February |

## Example Sentences

- **عِنْدي ثَلاثةُ كُتُبٍ.** (ʿindī thalāthatu kutubin.) — I have three books. (m. noun → f. number)
- **عِنْدي ثَلاثُ بَناتٍ.** (ʿindī thalāthu banātin.) — I have three girls. (f. noun → m. number)
- **السّاعة الآن الثّالِثة.** (as-sāʿatu l-āna ath-thālitha.) — It's now three o'clock.
- **اليَوْم الجُمُعة.** (al-yawmu l-jumuʿa.) — Today is Friday.
- **في شَهْر يَناير.** (fī shahri yanāyir.) — In January.

## Grammar Notes

- **Numerals are written left-to-right** even within RTL text.
- **Polarity rule**: with numbers 3-10, the number takes the gender opposite to the singular form of the counted noun.
- **Case agreement**: 1-2 = adjective form, 3-10 + genitive plural noun, 11-99 + accusative singular noun, 100+ + genitive singular noun.
- **The week starts on Sunday** in most Arab calendars.
- **Friday (الجُمُعة)** is the holy day; offices often close on Fri-Sat.

## Common Mistakes

- Forgetting polarity: ثلاث كتب is wrong — it should be ثلاثة كتب.
- Reading numbers RTL: read 2025 as "two thousand and twenty-five," LTR.
- Confusing سَنة (year) with سُنّة (Sunna, religious practice).

## Try It Yourself

1. Count 1-10 with a feminine noun (بنت) and a masculine noun (ولد).
2. Tell time: 1:00, 3:30, 5:15.
3. Say today's day and date.
4. List the days of the week from Sunday.

## Next Steps

Numbers and time set. Next: smooth conversational Arabic.

# Introductions & Polite Phrases

Arabic conversation is rich with set phrases for politeness, hospitality, and religious blessing. Mastering these chunks is the fastest route to natural-sounding Arabic.

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| اِسْمي … | ismī … | my name is … |
| ما اسْمُك؟ | mā ismuka/ki? | what's your name? (m / f) |
| تَشَرَّفْنا | tasharrafnā | pleased to meet you |
| من أين أنت؟ | min ayna anta/anti? | where are you from? |
| أنا من … | anā min … | I'm from … |
| أمريكا | Amrīkā | America |
| إنجلترا | Injiltrā | England |

| كَم عُمْرُك؟ | kam ʿumruka/ki? | how old are you? |
| عُمْري … سنة | ʿumrī … sana | I'm … years old |
| ماذا تَعْمَل؟ | mādhā taʿmal? | what do you do? |
| طالِب / طالِبة | ṭālib / ṭāliba | student (m / f) |
| مُهَنْدِس | muhandis | engineer |
| طَبيب | ṭabīb | doctor |
| من فَضْلِك | min faḍlika/ki | please |

| تَفَضَّل | tafaḍḍal | please / go ahead / help yourself |
| آسِف / آسِفة | āsif / āsifa | sorry (m / f) |

## Example Sentences

- **اِسْمي سارة. ما اسْمُك؟** (ismī Sāra. mā ismuka?) — My name is Sara. What's your name?
- **تَشَرَّفْنا، أنا أحمد.** (tasharrafnā, anā Aḥmad.) — Pleased to meet you, I'm Ahmad.
- **أنا من المَغْرِب، وأنت؟** (anā min al-Maghrib, wa-anta?) — I'm from Morocco, and you?
- **أتَكَلَّمُ العَرَبيّة قَليلاً.** (atakallamu l-ʿarabiyya qalīlan.) — I speak Arabic a little.
- **عُمْري عِشْرونَ سَنة.** (ʿumrī ʿishrūna sana.) — I'm 20 years old.
- **أنا طالِبة في الجامِعة.** (anā ṭāliba fī l-jāmiʿa.) — I'm a (female) student at the university.
- **من فَضْلِك، أَيْن المَطار؟** (min faḍlika, ayna l-maṭār?) — Excuse me, where's the airport?

## Grammar Notes

- Address suffixes: -ka for a man, -ki for a woman, -kum for a group. اسمُك becomes اسمُكَ or اسمُكِ in vocalized text.
- **تَفَضَّل** is hyper-polite, used for "please come in," "please take this," "go ahead."
- **Apologies** match gender: a woman says آسِفة, a man says آسِف.
- **Ask language proficiency**: هل تَتَكَلَّمُ الإنجليزيّة؟ (Do you speak English?)

## Common Mistakes

- Asking ما اسمُك؟ to a woman — change suffix: ما اسمُكِ؟
- Forgetting gender on آسِف.
- Saying "I am 20" as أنا عشرون — use عُمْري عشرون سنة.

## Try It Yourself

1. Introduce yourself in a 3-sentence dialogue.
2. Ask a stranger their name, where they're from, and their job.
3. Apologize as your gender.
4. Ask politely: Where's the bathroom? Where's the train station?

## Next Steps

Polite small talk done. Next: shopping, food, and travel.

# MSA vs Dialects Overview

Modern Standard Arabic (MSA, الفُصْحى) is used in news, books, formal speech, and pan-Arab communication. But day-to-day people speak local dialects (عامّيّة), which differ enough to confuse learners.

## What Is MSA?

- **الفُصْحى (al-fuṣḥā)** = "the most eloquent." Standardized form derived from Classical Arabic (the Qurʾān).
- Used in: newspapers, TV news, books, formal speeches, religious sermons, pan-Arab pop songs (sometimes).
- Nobody speaks it natively at home — you learn it in school.

## Major Dialect Families

| Dialect | Region | Notes |
|---------|--------|-------|
| Egyptian (مَصْري) | Egypt | Most-understood dialect; dominant in film/TV. |
| Levantine (شامي) | Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine | Soft, melodic; popular in dramas. |
| Gulf (خليجي) | Saudi, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain | Closer to MSA, deep "q" sound. |
| Iraqi (عراقي) | Iraq | Influenced by Persian and Turkish. |
| Maghrebi (مَغْرِبي) | Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya | Very different; French/Berber influence. Hard for outsiders. |
| Sudanese | Sudan | Distinct mixture. |
| Yemeni | Yemen | Conservative; preserves older features. |

## Quick Comparison: "How are you?"

| Variety | Phrase | romanization |
|---------|--------|--------------|
| MSA | كَيْفَ حالُك؟ | kayfa ḥāluk? |
| Egyptian | إزَّيَّك؟ | izzayyak? |
| Levantine | كيفك؟ | kīfak? |
| Gulf | شخبارك؟ | shkhbārak? |
| Maghrebi | كيداير؟ | kīdāyer? |

## Quick Comparison: "I want"

| Variety | Phrase |
|---------|--------|
| MSA | أُريدُ (urīdu) |
| Egyptian | عاوز / عايزة (ʿāwiz / ʿayza) |
| Levantine | بِدّي (biddī) |
| Gulf | أَبي / أَبا (abī / abā) |
| Maghrebi | بغيت (bghīt) |

## What's the Same?

- The script — all Arabic dialects use the same alphabet.
- Most core nouns: kitāb, bayt, walad, bint, mā, khubz.
- Numbers, prayer phrases (al-ḥamdu lillāh), religious vocabulary.

## What's Different?

- **Pronunciation**: ق becomes ʾ in Egyptian/Levantine, g in Gulf, q in Maghrebi.
- **Verbs**: present-tense markers differ. Egyptian uses بـ; Levantine uses بـ; Gulf uses none.
- **Vocabulary**: "now" — MSA الآن, Egyptian دلوقتي, Levantine هلّأ, Gulf الحين.
- **Negation**: MSA لا/ما, Egyptian مش/ما...ش, Levantine مش, Maghrebi ماش.

## Strategy for Learners

1. Start with **MSA** for reading, news, formal travel — universally understood.
2. Pick **one dialect** for daily speaking based on your goals (Egyptian = pop culture; Levantine = travel; Gulf = business).
3. Don't mix dialects mid-sentence — sounds odd.
4. Listen to dialect TV shows: Egyptian films, Lebanese/Syrian dramas, Khaleeji series.

## Common Mistakes

- Speaking pure MSA in casual conversation — sounds robotic, like Shakespearean English.
- Assuming all Arabs understand each other perfectly — Maghrebi is opaque to easterners.
- Using a dialect in a job interview — switch to MSA for formality.

## Try It Yourself

1. Watch one Egyptian film clip and one Levantine clip — note the differences.
2. Memorize "How are you?" in three varieties.
3. Identify the dialect of an Arabic song.

## Next Steps

You understand the landscape. Now sharpen reading.

# Reading Arabic Script

Reading authentic Arabic is initially slow because short vowels are usually omitted and four shapes per letter must be recognized in context. Practice rebuilds confidence quickly.

## Core Vocabulary (signs & headlines)

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| دُخول | dukhūl | entrance |
| خُروج | khurūj | exit |
| مَفْتوح | maftūḥ | open |
| مُغْلَق | mughlaq | closed |
| مَمْنوع | mamnūʿ | forbidden |
| تَحْذير | taḥdhīr | warning |
| الحَمّام | al-ḥammām | bathroom |
| رِجال / نِساء | rijāl / nisāʾ | men / women |
| مَطْعَم | maṭʿam | restaurant |
| مُسْتَشْفى | mustashfā | hospital |
| صَيْدَليّة | ṣaydaliyya | pharmacy |
| بَنْك | bank | bank |
| مَحَطّة | maḥaṭṭa | station |
| الجَريدة | al-jarīda | newspaper |
| العُنْوان | al-ʿunwān | the headline / address |

## Reading Strategies

- **Identify the root first**: scan a word for its three consonants and ignore prefixes/suffixes. مَكْتَبة → ك ت ب → "library."
- **Recognize prefixes**:
  - الـ — "the"
  - وَ — "and"
  - بِ — "with / by"
  - لِ — "for / to"
  - فَ — "and so / then"
- **Recognize suffixes**:
  - ـي — "my"
  - ـك / ـكِ — "your"
  - ـه / ـها — "his / her"
  - ـونَ / ـات — masculine / feminine plural
- **Newspaper headlines** drop short vowels but use familiar templates: المُدَرِّسُ (the teacher), التَّعْليمُ (education).

## Example Sentences

- **مَكْتَبةُ الجامِعة مَفْتوحة من ٩ إلى ٥.** — The university library is open from 9 to 5.
- **دُخول السَّيّارات مَمْنوع.** — Vehicle entry forbidden.
- **عُنْوان الجَريدة: "اِنْتِخابات جَديدة".** — Newspaper headline: "New elections."
- **هذا المَطْعَم يَفْتَحُ في السّاعة السّابِعة.** — This restaurant opens at 7.

## Common Mistakes

- Trying to read every short vowel — relax; native readers infer them.
- Confusing similar letter shapes (ب ت ث ن — same skeleton, different dots).
- Reading word-by-word — read in phrases (al-mudarrisu fī, "the teacher in").

## Try It Yourself

1. Open Al Jazeera Arabic and find 5 cognates / international words (تَكْنولوجيا, اِقْتِصاد, ديمقراطيّة).
2. Identify the root of: مَدْرَسة, طالِب, كاتِب, مَكْتَب.
3. Remove the prefix الـ and tell which letter doubles: الشَّمس, القَمَر, السَّمَك.
4. Read aloud one news headline.

## Next Steps

Reading and writing reinforce each other. Now write Arabic.

| Ruqʿah | الرُّقْعة | everyday handwriting |
| Thuluth | الثُّلُث | architectural, decorative |
| Diwani | الدّيواني | Ottoman official documents |
| Kufic | الكوفي | early Qurʾāns, modern logos |
| Maghrebi | المَغْرِبي | North African manuscripts |

Most learners write **Ruqʿah** by hand (fast, simple) and read **Naskh** in print.

## Example Sentences (formal letter)

- **عَزيزي أحمد،** — Dear Ahmad,
- **أتَمَنّى أن تكون بِخَيْر.** — I hope you are well.
- **أكتب لك من القاهرة.** — I'm writing to you from Cairo.
- **مَع التَّحيّات، سارة.** — With regards, Sara.

## Writing Rules

- **Right-to-left**: pen starts on the right edge.
- **Letters connect** from the right side except after non-connectors (ا د ذ ر ز و).
- **Dots are critical**: بـ ت ث differ only in dot count and position.
- **Diacritic marks** (taшkīl) sit above or below the letter — usually omitted in adult prose.
- **Punctuation is mirrored**: Arabic uses ، (Arabic comma) and ؟ (mirrored question mark).

## Common Mistakes

- Writing letters disconnected — Arabic letters bind into one shape per word.
- Misplacing dots — shifts ج (j) to خ (kh) to ح (ḥ).
- Using Latin punctuation — switch to Arabic ، ؛ ؟.

## Try It Yourself

1. Write a 5-line letter to a pen pal.
2. Practice connecting letters in: مَدْرَسة, طالِب, كِتاب, مَكْتَبة.
3. Sign a postcard: عَزيزتي + name + date.
4. Copy one short Qurʾānic verse in Naskh script.

## Next Steps

Now read longer texts with comprehension.

# Reading Comprehension

Moving beyond signs and short headlines to paragraphs requires strategy: scan for the topic sentence, identify the verb, and use root recognition to guess unknown words.

## Sample Text 1: News Snippet

**أعلنَتْ وَزارة الصِّحّة أمس أنَّ عَدَدَ الإصاباتِ في المُسْتَشْفياتِ قد اِنْخَفَضَ بِنِسْبةِ ١٠٪ خِلالَ الشَّهْرِ الماضي.**

(aʿlanat wizāratu ṣ-ṣiḥḥati amsi anna ʿadada l-iṣābāti fī l-mustashfayāti qad inkhafaḍa bi-nisbati 10% khilāla sh-shahri l-māḍī.)

> "The Ministry of Health announced yesterday that the number of cases in hospitals has dropped by 10% during the past month."

**Key vocabulary**: وزارة (ministry), الصِّحّة (health), أعلنَ (announced), إصابة (case/injury), اِنْخَفَضَ (decreased), نِسْبة (percentage).

## Sample Text 2: Story Opening

**كان يا ما كان في قَديمِ الزَّمان، رَجُلٌ فَقير يَعيشُ في قَرْية صَغيرة. كان لَهُ ثَلاثةُ أبناء.**

(kāna yā mā kāna fī qadīmi z-zamān, rajulun faqīrun yaʿīshu fī qaryatin ṣaghīra. kāna lahu thalāthatu abnāʾin.)

> "Once upon a time, there was a poor man who lived in a small village. He had three sons."

**Key vocabulary**: كان يا ما كان (once upon a time), قَديم الزَّمان (olden times), فَقير (poor), يَعيش (lives), قَرْية (village).

## Sample Text 3: Modern Conversation Snippet

**— مَرحَباً، هل أنت من القاهِرة؟**
**— لا، أنا من الإسْكَنْدَريّة، لكِنّي أَدْرُسُ في القاهِرة.**
**— ماذا تَدْرُس؟**
**— أَدْرُسُ الطِّبّ في جامِعةِ القاهِرة.**

> "— Hi, are you from Cairo?
> — No, I'm from Alexandria, but I study in Cairo.
> — What do you study?
> — I study medicine at Cairo University."

## Comprehension Strategies

- **Skim first** for known words and proper nouns. They anchor the topic.
- **Find the verb** — usually first in MSA verbal sentences. The verb's root + tense reveals action and time.
- **Use context for unknown words**: a word in a list of medical terms is probably medical.
- **Don't translate every word** — get the gist, then refine.

## Common Mistakes

- Reading word-by-word — too slow.
- Looking up every unknown word — kills flow.
- Misidentifying the subject because Arabic puts subjects after the verb.

## Try It Yourself

1. Read a paragraph from Al Jazeera and summarize in one English sentence.
2. Identify the main verb in each of the three sample texts above.
3. List 5 unknown words from a real article and look them up.
4. Read aloud Sample Text 2 with full taшkīl.

## Next Steps

Reading skills built. Now zoom out: Arab world geography.

# Arab World Geography & Diversity

The Arab world (الوَطَن العَرَبي) spans 22 countries from Morocco to Oman, ~440 million people. Its diversity — geographic, religious, ethnic, dialectal — defies any single image.

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| الوَطَن العَرَبي | al-waṭan al-ʿarabī | the Arab world |
| العالَم العَرَبي | al-ʿālam al-ʿarabī | the Arab world (alt.) |
| دَوْلة | dawla | state / country |

| الخَليج | al-khalīj | the Gulf |
| نيل | Nīl | the Nile |

## The 22 Arab League States (selection)

## Diversity Inside the Arab World

- **Languages**: Arabic is dominant, but Berber/Amazigh (Morocco, Algeria), Kurdish (Iraq, Syria), Nubian (Sudan), and dozens more are spoken.
- **Religions**: ~90% Muslim (Sunni majority, Shi'a strong in Iraq/Lebanon/Bahrain). Significant Christian populations: Coptic (Egypt), Maronite (Lebanon), Chaldean (Iraq), and others.
- **Geography**: deserts (Sahara, Empty Quarter), mountains (Atlas, Lebanon), rivers (Nile, Tigris, Euphrates), seas (Mediterranean, Red, Gulf).
- **Economies**: oil-rich Gulf vs agrarian Egypt vs tourism-driven Morocco.

## Example Sentences

- **مِصر أكبر دَوْلة عَرَبيّة بِالسُّكّان.** (Miṣr akbaru dawlatin ʿarabiyyatin bi-s-sukkān.) — Egypt is the most populous Arab country.
- **الرِّباط عاصِمة المَغْرِب.** (ar-Ribāṭ ʿāṣimat al-Maghrib.) — Rabat is the capital of Morocco.
- **يَمُرُّ نَهْرُ النيل بِمِصر والسودان.** — The Nile flows through Egypt and Sudan.

## Common Mistakes

- Treating "Arab" and "Muslim" as synonyms — most Muslims are not Arab (Indonesia, Pakistan, etc.).
- Calling Iran an Arab country — it's Persian.
- Calling Turkey an Arab country — it's Turkic.

## Try It Yourself

1. Locate 10 Arab countries on a map.
2. Match capital to country: Rabat, Doha, Beirut, Sanaa.
3. Name 3 Arab countries in Africa, 3 in the Levant, 3 in the Gulf.
4. List 3 non-Arabic languages spoken in the Arab world.

## Next Steps

Geography sets the stage. Next: Islamic culture and traditions.

# Islamic Culture & Traditions

Islam shapes much of Arab daily life — calendar, greetings, food, weekends, and ethics — even for non-Muslim Arabs. Knowing the basics is essential cultural literacy.

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| الإسلام | al-Islām | Islam ("submission") |
| مُسْلِم / مُسْلِمة | muslim / muslima | Muslim (m / f) |
| القُرْآن | al-Qurʾān | the Qurʾān |
| النَّبي مُحَمَّد | an-nabī Muḥammad | the Prophet Muhammad |
| الصَّلاة | aṣ-ṣalāh | prayer |
| المَسْجِد / الجامِع | al-masjid / al-jāmiʿ | mosque |
| رَمَضان | Ramaḍān | Ramadan (month of fasting) |
| الصَّوْم | aṣ-ṣawm | fasting |
| إفْطار | ifṭār | breaking fast (sunset meal) |
| سُحور | suḥūr | pre-dawn meal |
| العِيد | al-ʿīd | feast / holiday |
| عيد الفِطْر | ʿīd al-fiṭr | end-of-Ramadan feast |
| عيد الأَضْحى | ʿīd al-aḍḥā | feast of sacrifice |
| الحَجّ | al-ḥajj | pilgrimage to Mecca |
| الزَّكاة | az-zakāh | almsgiving |
| الشَّهادة | ash-shahāda | declaration of faith |
| حَلال | ḥalāl | permitted |
| حَرام | ḥarām | forbidden |
| إن شاء الله | in shāʾa llāh | God willing |
| الحَمْدُ لله | al-ḥamdu lillāh | praise be to God |
| ما شاء الله | mā shāʾa llāh | what God has willed (admiration) |
| بِسم الله | bismi llāh | in the name of God (before eating, etc.) |

## Five Pillars of Islam (أرْكان الإسلام)

1. **الشَّهادة** — declaration: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is His Messenger."
2. **الصَّلاة** — five daily prayers (fajr, ẓuhr, ʿaṣr, maghrib, ʿishāʾ).
3. **الزَّكاة** — annual giving of ~2.5% of wealth to the poor.
4. **الصَّوْم** — fasting from dawn to sunset during Ramadan.
5. **الحَجّ** — pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime if able.

## Example Sentences

- **رَمَضان كَريم!** (Ramaḍān karīm!) — "Ramadan generous!" (greeting)
- **رَمَضان مُبارَك!** (Ramaḍān mubārak!) — "Blessed Ramadan!"
- **عيد مُبارَك!** (ʿīd mubārak!) — "Blessed feast!"
- **في رَمَضان نَصومُ من الفَجْر إلى المَغْرِب.** — In Ramadan we fast from dawn to sunset.
- **نَذْهَبُ إلى المَسْجِد يَوْمَ الجُمُعة.** — We go to the mosque on Friday.

## Cultural Notes

- **Friday prayer (صلاة الجمعة)** is the main weekly congregational prayer; many countries have a Fri-Sat weekend.
- **Halal food**: meat slaughtered according to Islamic rules; pork and alcohol are forbidden.
- **Ramadan etiquette**: don't eat or drink in public during daylight; restaurants reopen at iftar.
- **Hospitality is religiously rooted**: refusing food at someone's home can offend.
- **Religious phrases pepper everyday speech**, even in non-religious contexts.

## Common Mistakes

- Assuming all Arabs are Muslim — significant Christian and other communities exist.
- Saying "Allah" only refers to "the Muslim god" — Arab Christians also say الله.
- Eating publicly during Ramadan in a Muslim country — is rude or even illegal.

## Try It Yourself

1. Greet someone during Ramadan correctly.
2. Memorize the five pillars in Arabic.
3. Use بسم الله before eating.
4. Identify halal vs ḥarām items in a fictional menu.

## Next Steps

Culture deepens. Next: Arabic literature and arts.

# Arabic Literature & Arts

Arabic literature spans 1,500 years — from pre-Islamic poetry to modern Nobel laureates. The arts (calligraphy, music, cinema) are equally vibrant and indispensable to cultural fluency.

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| أَدَب | adab | literature |
| شِعْر | shiʿr | poetry |
| شاعِر | shāʿir | poet |
| رِواية | riwāya | novel |
| رِوائي | riwāʾī | novelist |
| قِصّة قَصيرة | qiṣṣa qaṣīra | short story |
| مُؤَلِّف | muʾallif | author |
| كاتِب | kātib | writer |
| موسيقى | mūsīqā | music |
| أُغْنية | ughniya | song |
| مُطْرِب | muṭrib | singer |
| فيلم | fīlm | film |
| مُخْرِج | mukhrij | director |
| خَطّ عَرَبي | khaṭṭ ʿarabī | Arabic calligraphy |

## Key Names — Literature

- **Al-Mutanabbī (المُتَنَبّي)** (915-965): the most quoted Arabic poet ever.
- **Naguib Mahfouz (نَجيب مَحْفوظ)** (1911-2006): Egyptian, Nobel Prize 1988. Read *Cairo Trilogy* (الثُّلاثيّة).
- **Mahmoud Darwish (مَحْمود دَرْويش)** (1941-2008): Palestinian national poet.
- **Nizar Qabbani (نِزار قَبّاني)** (1923-1998): Syrian; love and political poetry.
- **Tayeb Salih (الطَّيِّب صالح)** (1929-2009): Sudanese; *Season of Migration to the North*.

## Key Names — Music

- **Umm Kulthūm (أُمّ كُلْثوم)** (1898-1975): Egypt's "Star of the East," voice of the Arab world.
- **Fairuz (فَيْروز)** (b. 1934): Lebanese singer, beloved across the Arab world.
- **Mohammed Abdel Wahab (مُحَمَّد عَبْد الوَهّاب)**: composer/singer.
- **Modern**: Amr Diab (Egypt), Nancy Ajram (Lebanon), Tamer Hosny (Egypt).

## Key Names — Cinema

- **Youssef Chahine (يوسف شاهين)**: Egyptian, *Al-Mohager*, *Cairo Station*.
- **Nadine Labaki**: Lebanese director, *Caramel*, *Capernaum*.
- **Hany Abu-Assad**: *Paradise Now*.

## Example Sentences

- **أُمّ كُلْثوم أَشْهَر مُغَنّية في تاريخ العَرَب.** — Umm Kulthum is the most famous singer in Arab history.
- **قَرَأْتُ "ثُلاثيّة القاهِرة" لِنَجيب مَحْفوظ.** — I read Mahfouz's *Cairo Trilogy*.
- **الخَطّ العَرَبي فَنّ جَميل.** — Arabic calligraphy is a beautiful art.

## Common Mistakes

- Treating Arabic poetry as old-fashioned only — it's actively performed and read.
- Confusing classical (pre-modern) and modern literature — different genres entirely.
- Ignoring calligraphy as decorative — it's a fine art with major schools.

## Try It Yourself

1. Listen to one Umm Kulthum song with lyrics in front of you.
2. Watch one Mahmoud Darwish poem recitation on YouTube.
3. Read 5 verses of Mutanabbī in translation, then in Arabic.
4. Identify the calligraphic script (Kufic, Naskh, Diwani) in three logos or signs.

## Next Steps

Cultural fluency grounded. Next: deepen grammar — past tense and verb forms.

# Past Tense & Verb Forms

Arabic has 10 derived verb forms (وَزن, "measures") built on a three-letter root by adding prefixes, doubling consonants, or inserting vowels. Each form has a predictable meaning shift.

## Past Tense Conjugation (Form I: كَتَبَ — to write)

| Pronoun | Form | romanization |
|---------|------|--------------|
| أنا | كَتَبْتُ | katabtu (I wrote) |
| أنتَ | كَتَبْتَ | katabta (you m. wrote) |
| أنتِ | كَتَبْتِ | katabti (you f. wrote) |
| هو | كَتَبَ | kataba (he wrote) |
| هي | كَتَبَتْ | katabat (she wrote) |
| نحن | كَتَبْنا | katabnā (we wrote) |
| أنتم | كَتَبْتُم | katabtum (you m.pl.) |
| أنتن | كَتَبْتُنَّ | katabtunna (you f.pl.) |
| هم | كَتَبوا | katabū (they m.) |
| هن | كَتَبْنَ | katabna (they f.) |

## The 10 Forms (using k-t-b root or other common roots)

| Form | Past | Present | Meaning shift |
|------|------|---------|---------------|
| I | كَتَبَ | يَكْتُبُ | basic action (wrote) |
| II | كَتَّبَ | يُكَتِّبُ | causative / intensive |
| III | كاتَبَ | يُكاتِبُ | reciprocal (correspond with) |
| IV | أَكْتَبَ | يُكْتِبُ | causative |
| V | تَكَتَّبَ | يَتَكَتَّبُ | reflexive of II |
| VI | تَكاتَبَ | يَتَكاتَبُ | reciprocal of III |
| VII | اِنْكَتَبَ | يَنْكَتِبُ | passive / reflexive |
| VIII | اِكْتَتَبَ | يَكْتَتِبُ | reflexive of I |
| IX | اِحْمَرَّ | يَحْمَرُّ | colors / defects |
| X | اِسْتَكْتَبَ | يَسْتَكْتِبُ | requesting / seeking |

## Form Examples (root د ر س — to study)

- **Form I**: دَرَسَ — "he studied"
- **Form II**: دَرَّسَ — "he taught" (caused others to study)
- **Form III**: دارَسَ — "he studied with someone"
- **Form V**: تَدَرَّسَ — "he was instructed"
- **Form X**: اِسْتَدْرَسَ — "he sought instruction"

## Example Sentences

- **كَتَبْتُ رِسالة أمس.** (katabtu risāla amsi.) — I wrote a letter yesterday.
- **دَرَّسَتْ في المَدْرَسة.** (darrasat fī l-madrasa.) — She taught at the school. (Form II)
- **اِسْتَخْدَمْنا الكُمْبيوتر.** (istakhdamnā l-kumbiyūtir.) — We used the computer. (Form X of خ د م "serve")
- **اِنْكَسَرَ الزُّجاج.** (inkasara z-zujāj.) — The glass broke. (Form VII passive)
- **تَكَلَّمَ معي.** (takallama maʿī.) — He spoke with me. (Form V)

## Grammar Notes

- **Form II doubles the middle radical** (shadda): دَرَسَ → دَرَّسَ. Adds intensity or causation.
- **Form III adds ا after the first radical**: implies mutual or directed action.
- **Form IV adds أ prefix in past**: causative.
- **Forms V-X mostly add prefixes** (تـ, اِنـ, اِسْتـ).
- **Pattern recognition is everything**: see مُسْتَخْدِم, recognize Form X active participle ("user").

## Common Mistakes

- Conjugating each form like Form I — endings are similar but the stem changes.
- Confusing Form II (causative) with Form V (reflexive of II): دَرَّسَ "taught" vs تَدَرَّسَ "was taught."
- Ignoring Form patterns when learning new verbs — half the battle is which form.

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate دَرَسَ (Form I) in past tense, all 10 persons.
2. Build Form II of ك ت ب → كَتَّبَ; guess meaning.
3. Identify forms in: أَكْرَمَ (IV), تَعَلَّمَ (V), اِسْتَقْبَلَ (X).
4. Pick a root and produce as many forms as you can recognize.

## Next Steps

Verb forms organized. Now grammar's other notorious set: case endings.

# Case Endings & Iʿrāb

Classical Arabic marks three cases — nominative, accusative, genitive — through final vowels (إعْراب, "iʿrāb"). These endings are written only in fully vocalized texts and pronounced in formal speech and Qurʾān recitation.

## The Three Cases (singular indefinite noun: كِتاب)

| Case | Ending | Example | Function |
|------|--------|---------|----------|
| Nominative (المَرْفوع) | ـٌ (-un) | كِتابٌ kitābun | subject, predicate |
| Accusative (المَنْصوب) | ـً (-an) | كِتاباً kitāban | direct object, adverbial |
| Genitive (المَجْرور) | ـٍ (-in) | كِتابٍ kitābin | after prepositions, possessor |

## Definite Endings (with الـ)

| Case | Ending | Example |
|------|--------|---------|
| Nominative | ـُ (-u) | الكِتابُ al-kitābu |
| Accusative | ـَ (-a) | الكِتابَ al-kitāba |
| Genitive | ـِ (-i) | الكِتابِ al-kitābi |

## Trigger Patterns

- **Nominative**: subject, predicate of nominal sentence, predicate of كانَ.
- **Accusative**: direct object of verb; predicate of إنَّ; adverbial expressions.
- **Genitive**: after prepositions (في, إلى, من, على); after another noun in iḍāfa (possession).

## Example Sentences

- **كَتَبَ الطّالِبُ كِتاباً جَديداً.** (kataba ṭ-ṭālibu kitāban jadīdan.) — The student wrote a new book.
  - الطّالِبُ — nom. (subject); كِتاباً — acc. (object); جَديداً — acc. (agreeing with كِتاباً).
- **في البَيْتِ.** (fī l-bayti.) — In the house. (genitive after في)
- **إنَّ المُدَرِّسَ ذَكِيٌّ.** (inna l-mudarrisa dhakiyyun.) — Indeed, the teacher is intelligent. (accusative after إنَّ)
- **كانَ الجَوُّ بارِداً.** (kāna l-jawwu bāridan.) — The weather was cold. (predicate of كان in accusative)

## Special Cases

- **Diptotes (ممنوع من الصرف)**: a class of nouns that take only ـُ (nom.) and ـَ (gen. & acc., no kasra) and never tanwīn. Includes most proper names (مُحَمَّد), broken plurals (مَدارِس), and adjectives of form أَفْعَل (أَكْبَر).
- **Iḍāfa**: in a noun + noun possession structure (e.g., كِتابُ الطّالِبِ — "the student's book"), only the second noun shows the genitive. The first never takes tanwīn.
- **Sound plural endings**:
  - Masculine: ـونَ (nom.) / ـينَ (acc. & gen.)
  - Feminine: ـاتٌ (nom.) / ـاتٍ (gen. & acc., usually no fatḥa)

## Common Mistakes

- Reading every ending in casual speech — modern spoken Arabic drops most case endings.
- Pronouncing tanwīn on definite (الـ) nouns — never co-occur.
- Misidentifying iḍāfa — first noun never takes الـ or tanwīn.

## Try It Yourself

1. Vocalize: الطّالِبُ يَدْرُسُ الكِتابَ في المَدْرَسةِ.
2. Identify cases: أُمُّ الطِّفلِ في البَيْتِ.
3. Build a sentence with إنَّ and check accusative.
4. Decline كِتاب in all three cases, definite and indefinite.

## Next Steps

Case-endings drill done. Next: iḍāfa (possessive chain) and adjective phrases.

# Iḍāfa & Adjective Phrases

The إضافة (iḍāfa) construction is Arabic's way of expressing possession or "X of Y" relationships. Adjectives, by contrast, must agree with the noun in four ways. Both are foundational.

## Iḍāfa Structure: Noun + Noun (in Genitive)

- **كِتابُ الطّالِبِ** (kitābu ṭ-ṭālibi) — "the student's book" (lit. "book of the student")
- **بابُ البَيْتِ** (bābu l-bayti) — the door of the house
- **مُدَرِّسةُ اللُّغةِ العَرَبيّةِ** (mudarrisatu l-lughati l-ʿarabiyya) — the teacher of the Arabic language

## Iḍāfa Rules

1. The first noun (المُضاف) is **never** prefixed with الـ and **never** takes tanwīn.
2. The second noun (المُضاف إليه) takes the genitive case; it can be definite or indefinite.
3. If the first noun is feminine ending in ـة, the ـة is pronounced -at: مُدَرِّسةُ → mudarrisatu.
4. Definiteness of the whole phrase comes from the second noun: كِتابُ طالِبٍ = "a student's book" (indefinite); كِتابُ الطّالِبِ = "the student's book" (definite).

## Adjective Agreement Rules

An adjective must match its noun in:
1. **Gender** (masc. / fem.)
2. **Number** (sg. / dual / pl.)
3. **Definiteness** (الـ or no الـ)
4. **Case** (nom. / acc. / gen.)

## Example Sentences

- **بَيْتٌ كَبيرٌ** (baytun kabīrun) — a big house (indef. + indef.)
- **البَيْتُ الكَبيرُ** (al-baytu l-kabīru) — the big house (def. + def.)
- **سَيّارةٌ سَريعةٌ** (sayyāratun sarīʿatun) — a fast car (fem. agreement)
- **الطّالِباتُ الجَديداتُ** (aṭ-ṭālibātu l-jadīdāt) — the new (female) students (pl. agreement)

## Iḍāfa + Adjective Combination

When an adjective describes the first noun in an iḍāfa, it goes **after the whole iḍāfa**:
- **بَيْتُ المُدَرِّسِ الكَبيرُ** = "the teacher's big house" (الكبير agrees with بَيْت)
- **بَيْتُ المُدَرِّسِ الكَبيرِ** = "the big teacher's house" (الكبير agrees with المُدَرِّس)

The case ending tells you which noun the adjective modifies.

## Inanimate Plural Agreement

Plural inanimate nouns take **feminine singular adjectives**, regardless of original gender:
- **الكُتُبُ الجَديدةُ** (al-kutubu l-jadīda) — the new books. (Not الجَديدونَ.)

## Common Mistakes

- Putting الـ on the first noun of iḍāfa — always wrong. الكِتابُ الطّالِبِ is incorrect.
- Failing to make adjectives agree on all four axes.
- Treating plural inanimate as masculine — should be feminine singular adjective.

## Try It Yourself

1. Build iḍāfas: "the man's car," "the city's gate," "Cairo University."
2. Add a definite adjective: "the new car of the man."
3. Decline: بَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ in all three cases.
4. Practice plural inanimate agreement: "the old books," "the new schools."

## Next Steps

You handle iḍāfa and adjective concord. Next: complex sentences.

# Complex Sentences & Conjunctions

Arabic builds longer thoughts with conjunctions, relative clauses, conditionals, and verbal nouns (مَصْدَر). Word order shifts to mark emphasis or topic.

## Core Conjunctions

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| وَ | wa | and |
| فَ | fa | and so / then |
| ثُمَّ | thumma | then (sequential) |
| لكن / لكِنَّ | lākin / lākinna | but |
| أو | aw | or |
| لأنَّ | li-anna | because |
| لِكَيْ / لِـ | li-kay / li- | in order to |
| إذا | idhā | if (real condition) |
| لو | law | if (hypothetical, contrary to fact) |
| عِنْدَما | ʿindamā | when |
| قَبْلَ أن | qabla an | before |
| بَعْدَ أن | baʿda an | after |
| الَّذي / الَّتي | alladhī / allatī | who / which (relative, m / f) |

## Example Sentences

- **ذَهَبْتُ إلى المَدْرَسةِ ثُمَّ إلى البَيْتِ.** (dhahabtu ilā l-madrasati thumma ilā l-bayt.) — I went to the school, then home.
- **أُحِبُّ القَهْوة لكِنّي أُفَضِّلُ الشّاي.** (uḥibbu l-qahwa lākinnī ufaḍḍilu sh-shāy.) — I love coffee, but I prefer tea.
- **لم أَذْهَبْ لأنّي مَريض.** (lam adhhab li-annī marīḍ.) — I didn't go because I'm sick.
- **إذا دَرَسْتَ، نَجَحْتَ.** (idhā darasta, najaḥta.) — If you study, you'll succeed.
- **لَو دَرَسْتُ، لَنَجَحْتُ.** (law darastu, la-najaḥtu.) — If I had studied, I would have succeeded.
- **الرَّجُلُ الَّذي يَتَكَلَّمُ هو أبي.** (ar-rajulu lladhī yatakallamu huwa abī.) — The man who is speaking is my father.

## Grammar Notes

- **إذا (idhā)** introduces a real, possible condition; usually past tense in both clauses.
- **لو (law)** introduces a contrary-to-fact (counterfactual) condition; uses past + لـ + past.
- **الَّذي / الَّتي**: relative pronouns. Used only for definite antecedents. Indefinite antecedents take no relative pronoun.
- **لأنَّ + suffix**: لأنّي ("because I"), لأنّك ("because you"), لأنَّه ("because he").
- **Verbal nouns (مَصادِر)**: every verb has a noun form (كَتَبَ → كِتابة, "writing"); used after prepositions.

## Common Mistakes

- Using الَّذي with an indefinite noun: رَجُلٌ الَّذي... is wrong.
- Confusing إذا (real if) with لو (counterfactual if).
- Forgetting لـ in the second clause of a لو-condition.

## Try It Yourself

1. Combine: "I have a friend. He lives in Egypt." → using الَّذي.
2. Translate: "If I had time, I would travel."
3. Use ثُمَّ to chain three actions in your day.
4. Build a verbal noun: قَرَأَ → قِراءة; use it: أُحِبُّ القِراءة.

## Next Steps

You can build long sentences. Next: formal Arabic and media language.

# Formal Arabic & Media Language

Newspapers, TV news, government documents, and academic writing use a high register of MSA with specific vocabulary, set phrases, and structural patterns. Recognizing them speeds reading enormously.

## Core Vocabulary — News

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| أَخْبار | akhbār | news |
| تَقْرير | taqrīr | report |
| مُراسِل | murāsil | correspondent |
| صَحيفة | ṣaḥīfa | newspaper |
| مَقالة | maqāla | article |
| رَئيس | raʾīs | president |
| وَزير | wazīr | minister |
| حُكومة | ḥukūma | government |
| البَرْلَمان | al-barlamān | parliament |
| اِنْتِخابات | intikhābāt | elections |
| اِقْتِصاد | iqtiṣād | economy |
| سياسة | siyāsa | politics / policy |
| اِجْتِماع | ijtimāʿ | meeting |
| مُؤْتَمَر | muʾtamar | conference |
| اِتِّفاقيّة | ittifāqiyya | agreement |
| أَزْمة | azma | crisis |
| حَرْب | ḥarb | war |
| سَلام | salām | peace |
| أَمْن | amn | security |
| مُجْتَمَع | mujtamaʿ | society |

## Set Phrases in News Arabic

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| أَعْلَنَ المَصْدَر أنَّ … | aʿlana l-maṣdaru anna … | The source announced that … |
| مِن المُتَوَقَّع أن … | min al-mutawaqqaʿi an … | It is expected that … |
| أَكَّدَ الرَّئيس … | akkada r-raʾīsu … | The president affirmed … |
| في تَصْريح صَحَفي | fī taṣrīḥin ṣaḥafiyyin | in a press statement |
| وَفْقاً لِـ | wafqan li- | according to |
| وَزارة الخارِجيّة | wizārat al-khārijiyya | Ministry of Foreign Affairs |
| الأُمَم المُتَّحِدة | al-umam al-muttaḥida | the United Nations |
| بَيان رَسْمي | bayān rasmī | official statement |

## Example Headlines

- **اِجْتِمَاع طارِئ لِمَجْلِسِ الأَمْن.** — Emergency meeting of the Security Council.
- **اِرْتِفاع أَسْعار النِّفط في الأَسْواق العالَميّة.** — Rise in oil prices in global markets.
- **الرَّئيس يَزور الأُرْدُن غَداً.** — The president to visit Jordan tomorrow.
- **تَوْقيع اِتِّفاقيّة جَديدة بَيْنَ البَلَدَيْن.** — Signing of a new agreement between the two countries.

## Reading Strategies for News

1. **Headlines drop verbs**: "Rise in oil prices" instead of "Oil prices rose."
2. **Look for the actor + verb at the start**: usually subject-verb-object in headlines.
3. **Numbers are LTR within RTL text**: read 2025 normally.
4. **Set phrases recur**: "according to" (وَفْقاً لِـ), "the source confirmed" (أَكَّدَ المَصْدَر).
5. **Country and organization names** are often loanwords with consistent spellings: واشِنْطُن, نيويورك, فيسبوك.

## Common Mistakes

- Translating word-for-word — set phrases must be parsed as units.
- Reading numbers right-to-left.
- Missing the verb in headlines because there isn't one.

## Try It Yourself

1. Read three Al Jazeera headlines and identify subject + action.
2. Memorize 5 set phrases.
3. Write a 3-sentence "news brief" on a topic.
4. Compare a headline in Arabic and English versions of the same article.

## Next Steps

Final stretch: prep for the Arabic proficiency exam.

# Arabic Proficiency Exam Prep

Two main standardized exams certify Arabic proficiency: ACTFL OPI (American) and the ALPT (Arabic Language Proficiency Test). Many universities also use ILR or CEFR-equivalent scales. The CIMA exam (France) certifies MSA on the CEFR scale.

## Major Exams

| Exam | Body | Scale | Notes |
|------|------|-------|-------|
| ACTFL OPI | American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages | Novice → Distinguished | Oral interview, ~30 min |
| ACTFL Reading / Listening | ACTFL | Same scale | Multiple-choice |
| ALPT | Arabic Language Proficiency Test (Arab Academy) | 0-100 | Reading, listening, grammar, writing |
| CIMA | Institut du Monde Arabe (Paris) | A1-C2 (CEFR) | MSA only; widely recognized in Europe |
| Defense Language Proficiency Test (DLPT) | US Government | ILR 0-5 | Used for federal jobs |

## Subtest Skills

1. **Reading (قِراءة)** — comprehension of news, narratives, and academic texts.
2. **Listening (اِسْتِماع)** — dialogues, news clips, lectures.
3. **Writing (كِتابة)** — letters, essays, summaries.
4. **Speaking (مُحادَثة)** — interviews, monologues, role-plays.
5. **Grammar (نَحْو) & Vocabulary (مُفْرَدات)** — multiple choice.

## CEFR-Equivalent Targets

| Level | Vocabulary | Skills |
|-------|------------|--------|
| A1 | ~500 words | Self-introduction, basic phrases |
| A2 | ~1,000 | Daily routines, simple narration |
| B1 | ~2,000 | Express opinions, narrate experiences |
| B2 | ~4,000 | Argue points, read modified news |
| C1 | ~8,000 | Discuss abstract topics, read literature |
| C2 | 12,000+ | Near-native; specialized texts |

## Core Vocabulary

| Arabic | romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| اِمْتِحان | imtiḥān | exam |
| اِخْتِبار | ikhtibār | test |
| نَتيجة | natīja | result |
| دَرَجة | daraja | grade / score |
| نَجَحَ | najaḥa | passed |
| رَسَبَ | rasaba | failed |
| اِسْتَعَدَّ لِـ | istaʿadda li- | prepared for |
| مُسْتَوى | mustawā | level |
| شَهادة | shahāda | certificate |

## Strategy Tips

- **Mock exams every two weeks**: real time pressure builds stamina.
- **For the speaking section**, structure answers: introduction → 2-3 points → conclusion. Use connectors (أَوَّلاً, ثانياً, أخيراً).
- **For writing**, master 3 templates: formal letter, descriptive essay, opinion essay.
- **Vocabulary by frequency**: drill the 1,000 most common Arabic words first.
- **News exposure daily**: one 5-minute Al Jazeera segment with transcript.
- **Don't skip handwriting** — many exams require legible Arabic by hand.

## Example Sentences

- **اِسْتَعْدَدْتُ لِلاِمْتِحانِ لِمُدَّةِ شَهْرَيْن.** — I prepared for the exam for two months.
- **حَصَلْتُ على دَرَجةِ مُمتاز.** — I got an "Excellent" grade.
- **أَدْرُسُ العَرَبيّةَ لِلْحُصول على شَهادة.** — I'm studying Arabic to obtain a certificate.

## Common Mistakes

- Studying only MSA when speaking exams allow dialect — check the exam's policy.
- Underpreparing the writing section — most failure points happen here.
- Ignoring official sample tests — formats vary by exam.

## Try It Yourself

1. Take a free ALPT or ACTFL sample test online.
2. Record a 2-minute monologue: "Tell me about your family."
3. Write a 150-word essay: "صِفْ مَدينَتك" ("Describe your city").
4. Identify your target CEFR level and find a sample.

## Next Steps

You now have a complete Arabic foundation: alphabet → roots → cases → verb forms → media register → exam-ready. Continued growth comes from immersion: read Mahfouz, watch Al Jazeera, message Arab speakers daily. بِالتَّوْفيق! (bi-t-tawfīq!) — Best of luck!
